name: Limb Isolation
description: Separate a limb from its supports and block its return to create passing, pinning, or submission-entry opportunities.
summary: Limb isolation separates an arm or leg from the torso, other limbs, or mat supports that help the opponent move and defend it.
overview: Control the shoulder or hip as well as the wrist or ankle. Place a barrier on the return route before changing grips or advancing position.
key_principles: Identify which contacts support the target limb.
Control the shoulder or hip as well as the endpoint.
Place a knee, shin, or other barrier on the reconnection route.
Keep your own base while moving closer to the isolated limb.

component_skills.description: Read what feeds the target limb its strength: connection to the torso, help from the opposite arm or leg, a post on the mat, and the orientation of the hips behind it.
Manage the shoulder or the hip so that endpoint control cannot simply be rotated away, treating a wrist or ankle grip as a handle rather than as the isolation itself.
Place a knee, shin, shoulder or head across the reconnection line so the elbow or knee cannot travel home without first moving your whole structure.
Break the opponent's defensive grips — hand clasp, gable grip, lapel or belt anchor — in the order that costs them the most support, then extract with the hips rather than the arms.
Move your hips and chest to the isolated side instead of pulling the limb toward you, so structure rather than arm strength holds the separation open.
Return an isolated elbow to the ribs or knee to the chest, re-orient the joint out of the attacker's lever line, and rebuild a post before ever attempting to withdraw the limb.
Recognize when the barrier has failed and the isolation is gone, and give the limb back early to keep position instead of chasing a finish into a scramble.

principle_relationships.description: Isolation is the deliberate removal of the opponent's connections, so you must be able to read which connections exist before you can strip any of them.
The elbow-knee connection is the defender's primary re-support; the attacker's isolation and the defender's reconnection are the same exchange read from opposite sides.
The hierarchy tells you which control point is worth taking; isolation is the mechanism that keeps that point once you have it.
A limb only becomes a usable lever after it is separated from its supports, so isolation supplies the conditions that leverage then exploits.
Hyperextension is the finishing stage isolation makes possible; applied to a still-connected limb it becomes a strength contest instead of a mechanical break.
Frames are the supports the defender rebuilds, so every successful frame is an isolation undone and every frame destroyed is an isolation begun.
Inside position decides who can build barriers, which in practice decides which player gets to choose the limb that will be isolated.

application_contexts.how_applied: Keep an elbow separated from the ribs to remove a defensive frame and prepare an armbar entry.
Use an overhook or arm drag to occupy the hand that would post on the sweep side.
Contain one leg between your own so the guard player cannot easily bring both knees back in front.
Trap one arm while maintaining chest contact to reduce the hands available for defensive grip fighting.

decision_framework.decision_point: Do I need a limb at all, or only position?
decision_framework.action: Decide whether isolating buys a pass, a sweep or a finish; if the position is available without it, take the position and leave the limb alone.

decision_framework.decision_point: Which limb is already least supported?
decision_framework.action: Target what the opponent has already committed — a reaching arm, a posted leg, an over-extended knee — rather than manufacturing a target from a neutral frame.

decision_framework.decision_point: What is feeding that limb strength?
decision_framework.action: Name the supports explicitly: torso connection, the opposite limb, a mat post, hip orientation. Remove them in the order that costs the opponent the most.

decision_framework.decision_point: Can I reach the proximal joint?
decision_framework.action: Establish shoulder or hip control first. If only the wrist or ankle is available, treat it as a handle to travel along, not as the isolation.
Build a barrier — knee, shin, shoulder or head — across the return path before advancing the attack by a single inch.
Check your own posts and hip line. If separating the limb costs you base, move your body closer to the target instead of pulling harder on it.
If the elbow reaches the ribs or the knees rejoin, release, re-take position, and re-enter rather than forcing a finish through a rebuilt structure.

decision_framework.decision_point: Am I the one being isolated?
decision_framework.action: Reconnect and re-orient before attempting withdrawal, and tap early if the joint is already loaded — pulling out of a good line finishes the attack for them.

common_errors.error: Holding only the wrist or ankle
common_errors.consequence: The opponent turns the shoulder or hip and reconnects the limb.
common_errors.correction: Control above the joint and use the endpoint as a handle.

common_errors.consequence: The limb reconnects as soon as you change grips or position.
common_errors.correction: Place a structural barrier on the return route before moving on.

common_errors.consequence: The opponent uses the gap to reverse or move into your space.
common_errors.correction: Bring your hips and chest toward the isolated side instead of extending your arms farther.

training_approaches.description: Start in a light top pin. One partner separates an elbow from the ribs while the other gently reconnects it; no submission grips. Reset on separation or reconnection and switch roles.
training_approaches.focus: Block the return route with body position.

training_approaches.description: Start in Headquarters Position. The passer contains one leg while the guard player slowly brings both knees back in front. Reset when the knees reconnect or the pass reaches a stable pin.

observable_behaviors: Names the supports keeping a partner's arm safe when the roll is paused
Controls the elbow rather than the wrist when drilling armbar entries
Reconnects the elbow to the ribs when caught instead of pulling the arm out
Recognizes when control is lost and resets rather than continuing
Builds a barrier before advancing a kimura or armbar against light resistance
Isolates one leg to pass rather than fighting both knees at once
Explains both the attacking and the defensive side of the same exchange
Releases an isolation that has failed without surrendering position
Maintains the isolation through position changes as the opponent turns and scrambles
Switches to a second target when the first reconnection route is defended
Uses isolation for sweeps and passes, not only for submissions
Keeps base while separating so the opponent cannot reverse the reach
Diagnoses why a partner's isolation fails from one look at the proximal joint
Times isolation to the opponent's own commitment instead of manufacturing a target
Trades an isolation for a better position deliberately, including releasing a finish
Teaches the exchange from both roles using examples across guard, pins and leg entanglements

related_content.name: Armbar
related_content.relationship: Requires the elbow separated from the ribs and the shoulder denied rotation before the lever exists.

related_content.name: Kimura
related_content.relationship: The model case: two hands isolate one shoulder while the torso is prevented from turning with it.

related_content.name: Kneebar
related_content.relationship: Isolates one leg from its partner and from the hips so the knee line can be attacked alone.

related_content.name: Americana
related_content.relationship: Pins the arm away from the ribs at the elbow; the finish fails entirely if the elbow reconnects.

related_content.name: Arm Triangle
related_content.relationship: Traps one arm across the neck so the isolated limb becomes part of the strangle structure.

related_content.name: Kimura Trap
related_content.relationship: A position defined purely by an isolated shoulder, from which attacks and transitions both branch.

related_content.name: Armbar Control
related_content.relationship: The holding position for a fully isolated arm, where barriers matter more than finishing pressure.

related_content.name: Headquarters Position
related_content.relationship: Leg isolation applied to passing — one knee held between the passer's legs so both cannot track together.

related_content.name: Crucifix
related_content.relationship: Both arms isolated by separate structures, producing submissions with minimal pressure.

related_content.name: Arm Drag
related_content.relationship: Removes a posting arm from its support, converting a defensive limb into an entry to the back.

related_content.name: Elbow-Knee Connection
related_content.relationship: The defender's reconnection standard; isolating a limb means breaking exactly this connection.

related_content.name: Levers
related_content.relationship: Supplies the mechanics that an isolated limb makes available.

related_content.name: Danaher Armbar System
related_content.relationship: A full system built on isolating the arm and denying reconnection before any finishing force is applied.

flashcards.question: What does limb isolation actually remove?
flashcards.answer: The limb's supports — its connection to the torso, help from the opposite limb, and any post on the mat — so that a small part of the opponent has to resist your whole body.

flashcards.question: Why is a wrist or ankle grip not an isolation?
flashcards.answer: The free shoulder or hip lets the opponent rotate and bring their whole body behind your grip; only control of the proximal joint prevents that rescue.

flashcards.question: How does a defender undo an isolation?
flashcards.answer: By reconnecting the elbow to the ribs or the knee to the chest, re-orienting the joint out of the attacker's lever line, and rebuilding a post — reconnection always before withdrawal.

flashcards.question: How does limb isolation apply to guard passing?
flashcards.answer: From Headquarters Position the passer isolates one leg between their own so the guard player's knees cannot track together; a pass is a leg separated, not only a body angled.

flashcards.question: Why is the kimura grip the model isolation?
flashcards.answer: Two of your hands control one of their shoulders while the torso is denied the rotation that would bring the arm back to support, satisfying every requirement of the principle at once.

flashcards.question: What error makes an isolation fail on the very next movement?
flashcards.answer: Separating the limb without building a barrier on the reconnection route — the elbow or knee travels home the instant you shift to advance the attack.

flashcards.question: Why is limb isolation a passing and sweeping principle, not only a submission principle?
flashcards.answer: Removing one posting arm makes a sweep unopposed and pinning one knee makes a pass available, so isolation buys position long before it buys a finish.

flashcards.question: What should you do when your barrier fails mid-attack?
flashcards.answer: Release the limb and re-take position rather than chasing the finish; a rebuilt structure will not break, and forcing it usually costs the position as well.

flashcards.question: Why can pulling a trapped arm free be dangerous?
flashcards.answer: Withdrawal against an aligned lever loads the joint further and effectively finishes the submission for the attacker; change the angle and reconnect instead, and tap early when the line is set.

flashcards.question: How does limb isolation show up in Back Control?
flashcards.answer: Gift-wrapping one arm removes half the defensive frame around the collar, so the choking arm meets one defending hand rather than two.

flashcards.question: Which of your own resources should hold an isolation?
flashcards.answer: Two or more of your limbs plus a structural barrier — a knee, shin, shoulder or head — against one of theirs, so structure rather than grip strength does the work.

flashcards.question: What should you control besides the limb itself?
flashcards.answer: The torso, because an opponent who can turn into you brings the isolated limb along with their body and arrives back on full support.

graph_applicability.rationale: Separating or reconnecting limbs affects frames, posts, grips, passes, sweeps, pins, and submissions from either side of every exchange.
